subject: Career
title: Managing Up: Communicating with Your Boss
description: A 1-minute de-risking session on Managing Up: Communicating with Your Boss.

hook.text: Your boss doesn't read your weekly update. She reads 50 others. The problem isn't her — it's your format.

buildup.text: Managing up means adapting your communication to your manager's preferences and constraints.

discovery.text: Some managers want details. Others want headlines. Know which type and deliver accordingly.

twist.text: The biggest mistake: bringing problems without solutions. Managers value people who think before they escalate.

climax.text: Format: 'Here's the situation. Here's what I recommend. Here's what I need from you.' Concise and actionable.

punchline.text: Make your boss's job easier and your career gets easier.

quiz.question: What does 'managing up' mean in workplace communication?
options: Adapting communication to your manager's preferences and constraints
Telling your boss what to do

details.summary: Managing up means proactively shaping how you communicate with your manager to align expectations, reduce friction, and increase visibility for your work. It involves understanding your boss's preferred communication style, decision-making process, and priorities.
details.whyItMatters: Your manager controls your access to resources, raises, and opportunities. Professionals who communicate upward effectively advance faster than equally talented peers who do not.
takeaways: Learn your manager's preferred communication channel and cadence
Bring solutions alongside problems in every escalation
Provide regular status updates before your boss has to ask

faq.question: How do I figure out my manager's preferred communication style?
faq.answer: Observe how they communicate with peers. Do they prefer email summaries or quick Slack messages? Do they like data or narrative? Ask directly in a one-on-one: 'How do you prefer I keep you updated?' Most managers appreciate the question and answer frankly.

faq.question: What should I do when my boss gives vague or contradictory instructions?
faq.answer: Paraphrase the instruction back in writing and ask for confirmation. For example, 'Just to confirm, you'd like me to prioritize X over Y and deliver by Friday. Correct?' This creates a clear record and surfaces misalignment before you invest significant effort.
